strengths: AutoSeg addresses a useful practical problem: segmentation without a user-specified vocabulary. Decoding localized subsets of BLIP features is a promising methodological contribution within the existing zero-guidance setting.

The strongest results show substantial improvements with the same segmentation backbone. On VOC, AutoSeg achieves 87.1 mIoU versus 41.1 for SAM + BLIP + X-Decoder (Table 3), while class-agnostic mIoU improves from 38.0 with plain BLIP captions to 71.8 (Table 1).

LAVE addresses a real difficulty in evaluating automatically generated labels. Its scores differ from manual-mapping scores by only 0.2–1.1 mIoU across four datasets, providing useful evidence for its practicality.

Experiments cover four datasets and several alternative pipelines. Clear pipeline figures, disclosed pretrained models and hyperparameters, evaluator pseudocode, and informative failure cases help readers understand the approach and its limitations.
weaknesses: LAVE needs stronger validation as an evaluation contribution. The supplementary prompts explicitly map 'stuff' to background, although Cityscapes, Context, and ADE20K annotate stuff categories. For the larger vocabularies, the evaluator relies on the LLM remembering dataset categories rather than receiving the actual label list. Exact-label overrides and aggregate agreement with manual mapping are reassuring, but do not establish correctness for synonyms, ambiguous labels, or individual classes.

The comparison with ZeroSeg does not clearly separate segmentation improvements from evaluator improvements. Table A7 shows that changing Sentence-BERT mapping to LAVE alone raises VOC performance by 13.2 points, yet the manuscript does not clearly establish whether ZeroSeg was reevaluated using LAVE. This matters particularly for the small Context advantage, 11.7 versus 11.4 mIoU. A shared mapping protocol is needed, alongside captioning baselines with comparable generation budgets.

Parameter selection and evaluation are insufficiently separated. Section 5.1 reports Bayesian optimization against VOC mIoU without specifying a disjoint tuning split, and the headline results select the best caption-cycle count from each dataset's reported sweep. Because caption generation and clustering are stochastic, fixed settings selected independently of evaluation and repeated-run uncertainty are needed to assess generalization and small performance differences.

The central claim of more precise, comprehensive open-ended recognition is supported mainly by selected visualizations and vocabulary counts. Mapping an incorrect fine-grained label to the correct coarse category can still receive full credit, and generating more distinct nouns does not establish their accuracy. A targeted audit of novel labels, omitted objects, and hallucinated categories would substantiate this claim. Task-level novelty also needs narrower positioning because the cited ZeroSeg already addresses segmentation without vocabulary input.

Several correctable inconsistencies impede reproduction. Equation 9 describes independent maximum-IoU assignments rather than the stated Hungarian matching; alignment between the two patch resolutions and handling of appended positional dimensions before frozen BLIP decoding need clarification. Table A6 reports 87.1 VOC mIoU with one captioning cycle, whereas Table 2 reports 85.3 for one cycle and 87.1 for ten. These issues should be resolved before the ablation evidence can be interpreted confidently.
